summary: IPv6 Neighbor Discovery uses multicast heavily and assumes that every node on a link is trusted. This informational document examines where that design is inefficient or unsuitable, such as in wireless networks or networks with untrusted nodes.

plainLanguage.summary: Shouting every question at the whole room works in a small friendly group, but not in a noisy hall. This looks at when IPv6's way of finding neighbors causes trouble.

subtitle: How IPv6 neighbor discovery breaks down and how to fix it in large or untrusted networks.

tldr.problem: IPv6 Neighbor Discovery (ND) was designed assuming a small, friendly link where multicast works well and all nodes are trustworthy. This assumption breaks in large wired networks, wireless networks, and public access networks.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC identifies 15 specific ND issues stemming from three root causes: multicast inefficiency, trusting all nodes, and on-demand neighbor cache creation. It catalogs over 20 existing mitigation solutions from prior RFCs and shows how host isolation—separating hosts into different subnets or links—addresses all three causes at once.
tldr.outcome: Network operators now have a unified reference showing which ND problems occur where and which mitigation solutions apply, enabling better deployment choices for wireless, large datacenter, and public networks.

today: RFC 9898 is Informational and serves as a consolidation of ND issues and solutions documented in over 20 prior RFCs. It was published in November 2025 and does not obsolete any standards. It is a reference guide for network operators and designers choosing mitigation strategies for IPv6 ND problems in their specific deployment scenarios.

sections.title: The Neighbor Discovery Problem
sections.content:
Neighbor Discovery (ND) is the IPv6 protocol that lets nodes on the same link discover each other and learn about routers. It is built into the IPv6 specification and is required for stateless address autoconfiguration (SLAAC).

ND uses multicast for many of its messages: Neighbor Solicitations (NS) to find a node's MAC address, Router Solicitations (RS) to find routers, and Router Advertisements (RA) to learn about prefixes. It also assumes that all nodes on a link are trustworthy—a node can send ND messages and other nodes will believe them.

These design choices worked well in the 1990s when IPv6 was standardized, in small wired networks with trusted users. But today, networks are larger, wireless is everywhere, and public WiFi networks contain untrusted devices. The RFC documents 15 distinct ND issues across two main categories: multicast inefficiency (especially in wireless and large networks) and security problems (when nodes cannot be trusted).
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC starts by asking: what goes wrong with IPv6 when you leave the small, friendly office and enter the real world?

sections.title: The 15 ND Issues and Their Root Causes
sections.content:
The RFC systematically catalogs 15 ND issues and traces them to three root causes:

Multicast Issues (Issues 1–7): Multicast ND messages (NS, RA, RS) can degrade performance by consuming bandwidth and battery (especially on mobile devices). In wireless networks, multicast is unreliable because there are no acknowledgments; a lost NS might not detect a duplicate address. Issues include LLA DAD and GUA DAD performance degradation, host battery drain from unsolicited RAs, and host address resolution performance issues.

Trusting-All-Nodes Issues (Issues 8–12): An attacker on the link can spoof the source address in ND messages, launch rogue router attacks, send spoofed redirects, or replay ND messages to disrupt the network. These attacks can prevent address configuration, redirect traffic, or cause denial of service.

Router-NCE-on-Demand Issues (Issues 13–15): When a router needs to forward to a destination it has not cached yet, it creates a Neighbor Cache Entry (NCE) on demand and sends a multicast NS. An attacker can send traffic to non-existent addresses to exhaust the router's NCE memory. Buffering for address resolution also adds forwarding delay. Additionally, the router cannot account for hosts until they trigger an NCE creation, making subscriber management difficult.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC asks three questions: (1) Why does multicast hurt? (2) What if someone lies? (3) What if the router has to guess? Each question leads to several practical problems.

sections.title: Existing Solutions and Their Coverage
sections.content:
The RFC inventories 15+ mitigation solutions from existing RFCs and shows which issues each one solves:

Mobile Broadband IPv6 (MBBv6): Used in 3GPP networks, this solution puts each host in a point-to-point link with the router (no MAC address needed) and assigns each host a unique /64 prefix. This addresses all three root causes and solves all 15 issues.

Fixed Broadband IPv6 (FBBv6): Similar approach for broadband access, either point-to-point or point-to-multipoint with DAD proxy and unique prefixes per host. Also solves all issues.

Unique Prefix Per Host (UPPH): Assigns each host a unique IPv6 prefix (via SLAAC or DHCPv6-PD). The router can proactively install forwarding entries, eliminating Router-NCE-on-demand. Hosts in different subnets route through the router, eliminating host-to-host address resolution. Solves issues from Router-NCE-on-demand and some from router multicast, but not host multicast or security issues without additional measures like Private VLAN.

Wireless ND (WiND): RFC 6775/8505/8928/8929 redefine ND for Low-Power and Lossy Networks. Hosts register addresses proactively with the router instead of waiting to be queried, and multicast is used only for router discovery. Solves all issues for LLNs.

Other solutions: The RFC also covers Scalable Address Resolution Protocol (SARP), ND optimization for TRILL, ND proxy in EVPN, Gratuitous Neighbor Discovery (GRAND), Source Address Validation Improvement (SAVI), Router Advertisement Guard (RA-Guard), and others, each addressing specific subsets of issues.
sections.plainLanguage: Rather than invent new solutions, the RFC shows that proven techniques from mobile networks, broadband, and low-power networks already solve the problems. The trick is knowing which solution to apply where.

sections.title: Host Isolation as a Unifying Principle
sections.content:
The RFC's key insight is that host isolation addresses all three root causes of ND issues. There are three isolation methods:

L3+L2 Isolation: Assign each host a unique /64 prefix (L3 isolation) and physically separate hosts so they cannot reach each other in Layer 2 (L2 isolation). This combines MBBv6, FBBv6, and UPPH strategies. All ND issues are prevented.

L3 Isolation Only: Assign unique prefixes (UPPH) but allow hosts to be on the same shared medium (Ethernet, WiFi). Hosts route through the router, eliminating Router-NCE-on-demand issues and host multicast. However, hosts are still in the same solicited-node multicast group, so host multicast to routers and security issues may occur without additional measures.

Partial L2 Isolation: Use L3 ND Proxy devices to represent groups of hosts to the rest of the network. Within each group, ND multicast is segmented. Each proxy handles DAD and address resolution for its group, reducing multicast scope. This is a middle ground between full isolation and shared links.

The RFC provides guidelines for when to apply each isolation method based on deployment context: wireless networks (WiND), mobile broadband (MBBv6), fixed broadband (FBBv6 with unique prefixes), large datacenters (UPPH), and public networks (SAVI/RA-Guard with isolation).
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of fixing every ND problem individually, the RFC shows that separating hosts is the master key: put each host on its own network path, and problems vanish.

sections.title: Deployment Guidance
sections.content:
The RFC concludes with practical guidance for network operators selecting among isolation methods:

For wireless networks: Use WiND (RFC 6775 family) to change host behavior—hosts register addresses instead of waiting to be discovered.

For mobile broadband: Use MBBv6 with P2P links and unique /64 prefixes per host (the standard in 3GPP).

For fixed broadband (GPON, DOCSIS): Use FBBv6 with either P2P links (full isolation) or P2MP with OLT blocking between access ports (partial isolation with DAD proxy).

For large shared networks (datacenters, university campuses): Use UPPH with unique /64 prefixes to each host/server, combined with additional Layer 2 measures (Private VLAN, port isolation, or proxy-based segmentation) if security is a concern.

For public access networks: Combine isolation (UPPH or L2 isolation) with SAVI and RA-Guard to validate source addresses and filter rogue router advertisements.

The document emphasizes that these are not new inventions—they are proven practices used in production networks for years. The RFC's contribution is unifying them under a common framework so operators can match their problem to the right solution.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC is a playbook: if you run a wireless network, do this. If you run a mobile network, do that. If you run a datacenter, do the other thing.
